passages.title: Repeated charges expose violence across borders
passages.summary: Amos is a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah. He speaks in the days of King Jeroboam of Israel. The LORD roars from Zion, and the pastures wither. Amos announces judgment on the nations around Israel. Damascus threshed Gilead with iron sledges. Gaza and Tyre sold whole communities to Edom. Edom chased his brother with a sword and showed no pity. Ammon ripped open pregnant women to gain more land.
passages.uncertainty: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

lds.text: What human costs do the repeated charges name?

contextNote.title: Repeated charges expose violence across borders
contextNote.text: Each message begins with the same formula of three wrongs and four. None of these nations is charged with breaking Israel’s law. They are charged with cruelty any people would know as wrong. Verse 9 says Tyre handed over a whole community to slavery. It also forgot a treaty of brotherhood. Every charge in the chapter names harm done to human beings. God holds nations to account for such acts.

passages.title: The accusation turns toward Israel's own worship
passages.summary: Amos continues with Moab, which burned the bones of Edom’s king. Then he turns to Judah, which rejected the LORD’s law. Last he turns to Israel itself. The people sell the innocent for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals. They trample the heads of the poor. They lie down beside altars on clothes taken as security for debts. They told the prophets not to speak. God will press them down like a loaded cart.
passages.uncertainty: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

lds.text: Why do garments and wine beside altars expose wrongdoing?

contextNote.title: The accusation turns toward Israel's own worship
contextNote.text: Amos’s hearers would have approved the judgments on their neighbors. The eighth message turns on them. Israel’s list is the longest, and it concerns everyday dealings. Verse 6 says people are sold into slavery over small debts. Verse 8 says cloaks taken in pledge are used at the shrines. Exodus 22:26–27 required such a cloak back by sunset. The worship is furnished with the goods of the poor.

passages.title: A chosen relationship increases responsibility
passages.summary: God speaks to the whole family he brought up from Egypt. He chose them alone of all the families of the earth. Therefore he will punish them for their sins. Amos asks a series of questions about cause and effect. A lion does not roar without prey. When the LORD speaks, a prophet must prophesy. Foreign peoples are called to witness the oppression in Samaria. The rich houses of winter and summer will be destroyed.
passages.uncertainty: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

lds.text: The 2026 lesson connects prophetic speech with receiving God’s instruction. Why does chosen belonging increase responsibility?

contextNote.title: A chosen relationship increases responsibility
contextNote.text: Verse 2 has a surprising “Therefore.” Israel might expect its special place to bring safety. God says it brings greater responsibility. Being chosen makes the people answerable. Verses 3–8 then defend Amos’s right to say so. Verse 9 calls foreigners to look at Samaria’s violence. Verse 15 names the many fine houses that will fall.

passages.title: Religious display continues without a changed response
passages.summary: Amos speaks to the wealthy women of Samaria who crush the poor. They will be led away with hooks. He tells the people, with irony, to go and sin at their shrines. They love to bring offerings and announce them. God sent hunger, drought, blight, plague, and ruin. After each one they did not return to him. So Israel must prepare to meet its God. He forms the mountains and creates the wind.
passages.uncertainty: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

lds.text: The lesson invites return to God during trials. It does not claim that God sends every personal trial. What remains unchanged throughout the repeated disasters?

contextNote.title: Religious display continues without a changed response
contextNote.text: Verses 4–5 describe worship that is busy and generous. The people “love” to do it. Verses 6–11 list five disasters. Each ends with the same line: “yet you haven’t returned to me.” “Cleanness of teeth” in verse 6 means nothing to eat. Much religious activity goes on, and no one turns. Verse 12 says the next meeting will be with God himself.

passages.title: Justice must replace confidence in protected worship
passages.summary: Amos sings a funeral song for Israel. God tells the people to seek him and live. They turn justice into bitterness and hate anyone who speaks truth in court. They tax the poor and take bribes. They should hate evil and set up justice at the gate. The day of the LORD will be darkness and not light. God says he hates their feasts and will not hear their songs. He wants justice to roll like a river.
passages.uncertainty: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

lds.text: The lesson studies seeking God and choosing good as a path toward life. How do unfair courts explain the rejection of festivals?

contextNote.title: Justice must replace confidence in protected worship
contextNote.text: The “gate” in verses 10, 12, and 15 is the town’s court. Bribes are taken there, and the needy are turned away. Verses 21–23 then reject the people’s feasts and music. The two belong together. Unfair courts make the worship unwelcome. Verse 24 asks for justice like a stream that never dries. Many streams in that land ran only after rain.

passages.title: Comfort without grief becomes the first captivity
passages.summary: Amos warns those who feel safe in Zion and Samaria. They are the leading men of the first of the nations. They lie on beds of ivory and eat choice lambs. They sing to the harp and drink wine by the bowlful. They do not grieve over the ruin of their people. So they will be the first to go into exile. God hates Jacob’s pride and will give up the city. They have turned justice into poison.
passages.uncertainty: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

lds.text: What suffering do the comfortable leaders refuse to grieve?

contextNote.title: Comfort without grief becomes the first captivity
contextNote.text: Verses 4–6 list ivory beds, fine meat, music, wine, and oil. The charge comes in the last line of verse 6. These people feel no grief for the breaking of their nation. Their comfort has made them numb. The penalty fits the description. Verse 1 calls them the “first” of the nations. Verse 7 says they will go “first” into exile.

passages.title: The priest's royal protection conflicts with Amos's calling
passages.summary: God shows Amos a swarm of locusts and then a fire. Each time Amos pleads, and God relents. Then God shows him a plumb line set among the people. He will spare them no longer. Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, reports Amos to the king. He tells Amos to go home to Judah and earn his bread there. Amos answers that he was a herdsman and tended fig trees. The LORD took him from the flock and sent him.
passages.uncertainty: Selected places are not mapped in this chapter. No precise royal sanctuary location is assigned.

lds.text: The lesson studies Amos’s calling as an example of God speaking through prophets. Why does Amaziah call Bethel the king’s sanctuary?

contextNote.title: The priest's royal protection conflicts with Amos's calling
contextNote.text: Amaziah’s words show how he thinks. Verse 13 calls Bethel “the king’s sanctuary” and a royal house. Verse 12 treats prophecy as a way to earn bread. Amos answers that he never held that post. He kept flocks and tended trees. Verse 15 says the LORD “took” him, as he took David from the sheep. In verses 2 and 5 this same man pleaded for Israel.

passages.title: Dishonest markets prepare a different kind of famine
passages.summary: God shows Amos a basket of ripe summer fruit. The end has come for Israel. Amos speaks to those who trample the needy. They ask when the holy day will be over so they can sell grain. They shrink the measure, raise the price, and use false scales. They buy the poor for silver and sell the sweepings as wheat. God swears he will not forget. A famine is coming, a hunger to hear the LORD’s words.
passages.uncertainty: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

lds.text: The lesson applies hunger for God’s words to spiritual life. It also connects this image with the later Apostasy and Restoration. How do false measures connect trade with loss of freedom?

contextNote.title: Dishonest markets prepare a different kind of famine
contextNote.text: The merchants in verse 5 keep the new moon and the Sabbath. They only wish the days would end. The verse names three frauds in one sale. The measure is small, the weight for payment is heavy, and the scale is rigged. Verse 6 adds that they sell the chaff. They observe the holy day and defeat its purpose. Verses 11–12 take away the word they would not hear.

passages.title: Destroyed false security gives way to inhabited land
passages.summary: Amos sees the Lord standing beside the altar. He orders the temple struck, and no one will escape. Israel is no different to him than distant peoples. He brought the Philistines and Syrians from other lands too. He will sift Israel like grain and not destroy it completely. Then he will raise up David’s fallen shelter. The people will rebuild their ruined cities and live in them. They will never again be uprooted from their land.
passages.uncertainty: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

lds.text: How do inhabited cities reverse earlier warnings about lost houses?

contextNote.title: Destroyed false security gives way to inhabited land
contextNote.text: Verse 7 removes Israel’s claim to special treatment. God moved other nations as well. After that, the book ends in promise. In 5:11 the people built houses they would not live in. They planted vineyards and would not drink the wine. Verse 14 reverses both lines exactly. Verse 11 calls David’s house a “tent,” a humble thing raised again.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Aleppo–Euphrates approach
ancientRoads.summary: This road linked Aleppo with the Euphrates crossing near Til Barsip. Assyria’s state road began there.
ancientRoads.detail: Assyrian records and studies of ancient land support this route. It went through the Sajur and Manbij area. It then crossed the Jabbul plain toward Aleppo.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection and principal approach are well supported. The displayed bends simplify several local valleys and possible parallel tracks.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian King’s Road to Nineveh
ancientRoads.summary: The Neo-Assyrian state road connected western lands with the Assyrian heartland. It ended at the capital city of Nineveh.
ancientRoads.detail: The route crossed the Euphrates at Til Barsip. It crossed the Balih south of Harran. It also crossed Habur streams between Guzana and Nasibina. It then reached the Tigris at Nineveh. Royal messengers changed mules at road stations.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The named crossings and stations are well supported. The line between them is a broad regional path, not a surveyed roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian Tigris route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route followed the Tigris. It linked Nineveh, Kalhu, and Assur in the Assyrian heartland.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu held a central position between Assur and Nineveh. It supported long trips by land and river. Kalhu later became an Assyrian royal capital.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The cities and their connection are well supported. The line shows a broad route. It does not separate land travel from river travel at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Arbela–Babylonia route
ancientRoads.summary: An eastern branch connected Kalhu with Arbela. It followed the western edge of the Zagros Mountains. Other routes continued south into Babylonia.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu controlled an eastward route through Arbela. The route followed the western edge of the Zagros toward Babylonia. It avoided a direct crossing of the central desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is supported, but the precise southern alignment and stations are uncertain. The line is dashed.

regions.name: Kingdom of Israel · approximate
regions.summary: Ten tribes followed Jeroboam and formed a northern kingdom. Samaria became its capital under Omri.
regions.detail: Kings and Chronicles follow its kings beside Judah’s. Assyria takes Samaria and deports its people in 2 Kings 17.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Its borders with Aram, Moab, and Judah moved often.

regions.name: Kingdom of Judah · approximate
regions.summary: Judah was the southern kingdom. David’s family ruled it from Jerusalem for about four centuries.
regions.detail: Judah keeps David’s line when the north breaks away. Its kings fight Israel, pay it, and join it by turns.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It is not a border for one year.

regions.name: Aram of Damascus · approximate
regions.summary: Aram was a kingdom centered on Damascus. Assyria ended it in 732 BCE.
regions.detail: Ben Hadad and Hazael fight Israel for Gilead. Naaman, healed in 2 Kings 5, commands Aram’s army.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Aram and Israel traded control of Gilead and Bashan.

regions.name: Phoenician cities · approximate
regions.summary: Tyre, Sidon, and other coast cities each had their own king. They lived by ships and trade.
regions.detail: Ahab marries Jezebel, daughter of the king of the Sidonians (1 Kings 16:31). Elijah stays with a widow at Zarephath near Sidon.
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins separate cities along one coast. They were never one kingdom.

regions.name: Philistine cities · approximate
regions.summary: Five Philistine cities held the southern coast: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, and Gath.
regions.detail: Philistine towns sit on Judah’s western border. Israel besieges Gibbethon, a Philistine town, twice in 1 Kings 15–16.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Each city had its own ruler.

regions.name: Ammon · approximate
regions.summary: Ammon was a kingdom east of the Jordan. Its chief city was Rabbah, now Amman.
regions.detail: Ammon joins Moab against Jehoshaphat in 2 Chronicles 20. Amos 1 accuses Ammon of cruelty in Gilead.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the land around Rabbah.

regions.name: Moab · approximate
regions.summary: Moab was a kingdom on the high land east of the Dead Sea. Dibon was its capital.
regions.detail: Mesha king of Moab rebels after Ahab dies (2 Kings 3). A stone that Mesha set up tells his side.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Numbers 21:26 says Moab once lost land north of the Arnon.

regions.name: Edom · approximate
regions.summary: Edom was a kingdom south of the Dead Sea. The Bible calls its people the children of Esau.
regions.detail: Edom revolts against Judah in the days of Jehoram (2 Kings 8:20–22). Amos 1 accuses Edom of chasing his brother with the sword.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Edom’s people later moved west into southern Judah.

regions.name: Egypt · approximate
regions.summary: Egypt’s kings ruled the Nile valley and delta.
regions.detail: Shishak king of Egypt takes the temple treasures from Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:25–26). Hosea warns Israel against calling on Egypt.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Egypt’s ruling families and power changed across these centuries.

regions.name: Assyria · home region
regions.summary: Assyria’s home lay on the upper Tigris around Assur, Kalhu, and Nineveh. From 745 BCE its kings pushed hard to the west.
regions.detail: Menahem of Israel and Ahaz of Judah pay Assyria’s kings. Assyria takes Damascus, then Samaria, in 2 Kings 16–17.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows only the home region. Assyria’s reach to the west grew and shrank.

guides.title: Amos: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: The accusation turns toward Israel's own worship
steps.text: Amos’s hearers would have approved the judgments on their neighbors. The eighth message turns on them. Israel’s list is the longest, and it concerns everyday dealings. Verse 6 says people are sold into slavery over small debts. Verse 8 says cloaks taken in pledge are used at the shrines. Exodus 22:26–27 required such a cloak back by sunset. The worship is furnished with the goods of the poor.

steps.title: Justice must replace confidence in protected worship
steps.text: The “gate” in verses 10, 12, and 15 is the town’s court. Bribes are taken there, and the needy are turned away. Verses 21–23 then reject the people’s feasts and music. The two belong together. Unfair courts make the worship unwelcome. Verse 24 asks for justice like a stream that never dries. Many streams in that land ran only after rain.

steps.title: Dishonest markets prepare a different kind of famine
steps.text: The merchants in verse 5 keep the new moon and the Sabbath. They only wish the days would end. The verse names three frauds in one sale. The measure is small, the weight for payment is heavy, and the scale is rigged. Verse 6 adds that they sell the chaff. They observe the holy day and defeat its purpose. Verses 11–12 take away the word they would not hear.

chapterMaps.narrative: Amos is a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah. He speaks in the days of King Jeroboam of Israel. The LORD roars from Zion, and the pastures wither. Amos announces judgment on the nations around Israel. Damascus threshed Gilead with iron sledges. Gaza and Tyre sold whole communities to Edom. Edom chased his brother with a sword and showed no pity. Ammon ripped open pregnant women to gain more land.
chapterMaps.limits: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

chapterMaps.note: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.
chapterMaps.narrative: Amos continues with Moab, which burned the bones of Edom’s king. Then he turns to Judah, which rejected the LORD’s law. Last he turns to Israel itself. The people sell the innocent for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals. They trample the heads of the poor. They lie down beside altars on clothes taken as security for debts. They told the prophets not to speak. God will press them down like a loaded cart.
chapterMaps.limits: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

chapterMaps.note: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.
chapterMaps.narrative: God speaks to the whole family he brought up from Egypt. He chose them alone of all the families of the earth. Therefore he will punish them for their sins. Amos asks a series of questions about cause and effect. A lion does not roar without prey. When the LORD speaks, a prophet must prophesy. Foreign peoples are called to witness the oppression in Samaria. The rich houses of winter and summer will be destroyed.
chapterMaps.limits: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

chapterMaps.note: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.
chapterMaps.narrative: Amos speaks to the wealthy women of Samaria who crush the poor. They will be led away with hooks. He tells the people, with irony, to go and sin at their shrines. They love to bring offerings and announce them. God sent hunger, drought, blight, plague, and ruin. After each one they did not return to him. So Israel must prepare to meet its God. He forms the mountains and creates the wind.
chapterMaps.limits: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

chapterMaps.note: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.
chapterMaps.narrative: Amos sings a funeral song for Israel. God tells the people to seek him and live. They turn justice into bitterness and hate anyone who speaks truth in court. They tax the poor and take bribes. They should hate evil and set up justice at the gate. The day of the LORD will be darkness and not light. God says he hates their feasts and will not hear their songs. He wants justice to roll like a river.
chapterMaps.limits: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

chapterMaps.note: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.
chapterMaps.narrative: Amos warns those who feel safe in Zion and Samaria. They are the leading men of the first of the nations. They lie on beds of ivory and eat choice lambs. They sing to the harp and drink wine by the bowlful. They do not grieve over the ruin of their people. So they will be the first to go into exile. God hates Jacob’s pride and will give up the city. They have turned justice into poison.
chapterMaps.limits: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

chapterMaps.note: Selected places are not mapped in this chapter. No precise royal sanctuary location is assigned.
chapterMaps.narrative: God shows Amos a swarm of locusts and then a fire. Each time Amos pleads, and God relents. Then God shows him a plumb line set among the people. He will spare them no longer. Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, reports Amos to the king. He tells Amos to go home to Judah and earn his bread there. Amos answers that he was a herdsman and tended fig trees. The LORD took him from the flock and sent him.
chapterMaps.limits: Selected places are not mapped in this chapter. No precise royal sanctuary location is assigned.

chapterMaps.note: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.
chapterMaps.narrative: God shows Amos a basket of ripe summer fruit. The end has come for Israel. Amos speaks to those who trample the needy. They ask when the holy day will be over so they can sell grain. They shrink the measure, raise the price, and use false scales. They buy the poor for silver and sell the sweepings as wheat. God swears he will not forget. A famine is coming, a hunger to hear the LORD’s words.
chapterMaps.limits: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.

chapterMaps.note: Selected named references have approximate markers. Warnings do not establish traveled routes.
chapterMaps.narrative: Amos sees the Lord standing beside the altar. He orders the temple struck, and no one will escape. Israel is no different to him than distant peoples. He brought the Philistines and Syrians from other lands too. He will sift Israel like grain and not destroy it completely. Then he will raise up David’s fallen shelter. The people will rebuild their ruined cities and live in them. They will never again be uprooted from their land.
